explanation: Because branches are just 41 bytes, creating a branch takes microseconds and uses no disk space.
tip: Never hesitate to create branches — they are practically free!

explanation: `-c` stands for create. `git switch -c feature/x` is the cleanest modern syntax.

tip: Add `-v` to see the latest commit on each branch: `git branch -v`.

explanation: If HEAD points directly to a commit hash instead of a branch name, you are in 'detached HEAD' state.
tip: Always make sure HEAD points to a branch before making new commits.

explanation: Group prefixes (`feature/`, `bugfix/`) help tools and teammates organize work.
tip: Include the issue number if applicable: `feature/issue-42-auth`.

explanation: `git switch` was added in Git 2.23 to separate branch switching from file restoring.
tip: Switch switches branches; restore restores files.

explanation: Your editor will automatically refresh to show files on the active branch.
tip: Don't panic when files 'disappear' — switch back and they return!

explanation: Use `git stash` to temporarily shelf unfinished work, switch branches, and `git stash pop` later.
tip: Stashing is Git's clipboard for uncommitted code.

explanation: `-a` shows local and remote tracking branches (usually in red).
tip: Run `git fetch` first to ensure your remote branch list is fresh.

explanation: Publishes the branch so teammates can see it or review a PR on GitHub.
tip: Once pushed, GitHub will display a button to 'Compare & pull request'.
